parent.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. e4 dxe4 3. Nc3 Nf6
parent.overview: White offers a pawn with 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3, aiming for rapid development, the open f-file and a kingside attack with Bc4, Nge2 or Bf4, castling, g4/h4 and Qe1-h4 ideas against h7. Black accepts with 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 and can choose among the Euwe (5...e6), Ziegler (5...c6), Teichmann (5...Bg4) and Bogoljubov (5...g6) defences, or decline with the Lemberger Countergambit 3...e5. With accurate defence Black consolidates the pawn, trades pieces and heads for a better endgame; engines and master opinion call White's compensation insufficient, which is why it is almost never seen at top level. Below master level it scores very well because the attack is easy to play and hard to defend against. The game is typically open and tactical.

parent.name: Benoni Defense: Old Benoni
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...c5 before committing to ...d5 or ...Nf6; the root is a crossroads. White normally replies 2.d5, gaining space with a wedge, and Black then has to undermine d5 with ...e6, ...e5, ...d6, ...Nf6 or ...b5 so as not to be squeezed. Main branches are 2.d5 e6 (heading for a Modern Benoni structure), 2.d5 d6 3.e4 (the Schmid Benoni, with a King's-Indian-like set-up), and 2.d5 e5 (Czech Benoni, a locked centre with kingside play by f4 and queenside b4 for White). White can also play 2.dxc5, 2.e3 or 2.c3, which tend to transpose to other structures. Sources describe the opening as a long strategic space-versus-counterplay struggle, playable but demanding, rare at top level though used by Alekhine, Kasparov, Torre and Vaganian.

parent.name: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. O-O
parent.overview: 3...a6 is the main road of the Ruy Lopez (roughly two thirds to 90 per cent of Ruy games per the sources). It asks White's bishop an immediate question: Bxc6 (Exchange) or the retreat 4.Ba4, after which Black can play ...b5 to kick the bishop again. The main line is the Closed Ruy (5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3), a locked, slow centre where White builds the c3-d4 pawn duo and reroutes the knight Nb1-d2-f1-g3, and Black seeks queenside counterplay with ...c5/...c4 or ...Bb7 and ...Re8/...Bf8. Alternatives at move five or later include the Open Variation (5...Nxe4), the Arkhangelsk (5...b5), and Marshall Attack (8...d5), with Anti-Marshall systems used by White to dodge it. Play is typically slow positional manoeuvring (the 'Spanish torture': a small White edge pressed for forty moves) with very deep theory. It has been a main weapon of nearly every world champion.

parent.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defense
parent.moves: 1. Nf3 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. g3 a6
parent.overview: 1.c4 Nf6 is a crossroads, not a single structure. Black develops a piece, covers e4 and d5, and waits to see whether White wants d4 (which usually transposes into the King's Indian, Nimzo-Indian, Queen's Indian or Grünfeld) or a pure English set-up. The main branches are 2.Nc3 (with ...e6 giving Nimzo or Hedgehog-type play, ...g6 a King's Indian set-up, ...d5 a reversed Grünfeld, ...c5 or ...e5 symmetrical or reversed-Sicilian structures), 2.g3 and 2.Nf3. The typical English middlegame is a manoeuvring game with White's pressure on d5 and queenside space against Black's central break (...d5 or ...e5), but 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 (Mikėnas-Carls) can be sharper. Black's choice of branch decides almost everything about character and structure.

parent.name: Van Geet Opening
parent.overview: White develops a knight to c3, controlling e4 and d5, and keeps the pawn structure undecided to choose a set-up once Black replies. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so Queen's Gambit and English structures are not available without reorganising. Main replies: 1...d5 (the cleanest; 2.e4 transposes to obscure Scandinavian lines, or the Van Geet Attack after 2...d4 3.Nce2), 1...e5 (then 2.e4 Vienna Game, the most common transposition in the database, or 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Napoleon Attack), 1...Nf6 (one of the most unpleasant replies for White) and 1...c5 (transposing to Closed Sicilian or inferior-placed-knight lines). Sources call it sound and low-theory but unambitious: Black equalises with accurate play, so it earns points from surprise rather than from an edge, and masters play it under 1% of the time, though some strong correspondence players use it. The database root has few games itself; most of the subtree (about 290M games) is Vienna, Closed Sicilian and Chigorin-style transpositions that play like those openings.

parent.name: English Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...b6 (or 1...e6 2.c4 b6) intending ...Bb7, a hypermodern set-up in which the bishop on b7 pressures e4 and the centre rather than occupying it. After 3.e4 Bb7 White builds a broad pawn centre (Bd3, f3, Nc3) and Black undermines it with ...Bb4(+), ...f5 and sometimes ...Qh4, as in Polugaevsky-Korchnoi 1977 (4.Qc2 Qh4 5.Nd2 Bb4). The play is double-edged: Black gives White space and a strong centre, then goes for counterplay and tactics against it. Gambit versions (Hartlaub 4...f5, Polli 4.f3 f5) and 3.Nc3 Bb4 transpositions to a ...b6 Nimzo-Indian are the main branches. It was a surprise weapon of Speelman, Short, Miles and Keene in the 1980s and is rare in elite play, although some club players use 1...b6/2...Bb7 as a universal system.

parent.name: Mieses Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.d3, releasing the c1-bishop and making only a modest claim on the centre, and usually heads for an Indian-type set-up with g3, Nf3, Bg2 and short castling, then strikes with e4 (or c4). It generally transposes to the King's Indian Attack (after g3 and Nf3), the Closed Sicilian, or to colour-reversed Pirc, Modern or Philidor structures, so Black can occupy the centre with ...d5 and ...e5 and develop comfortably. Chess Doctrine calls it objectively passive: Black equalises quickly, theory load is minimal, and it is mainly a surprise weapon in rapid and blitz. Kasparov chose it against Deep Blue in 1997 (Game 3) to avoid computer preparation, but at grandmaster level it remains the exception. The play is closed and manoeuvring.

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.
